email.body:
She suggested a wedding video: something that would let those couples see a wedding at the venue before they could visit themselves.

Our team proposed a supplemental email for the couples with later appointments. It could share the footage ahead of the tour and give them an earlier glimpse of the experience they were coming to see.

What stood out to me was the opportunity in that interval. The couple had already taken a meaningful step by arranging a visit. There was still room to help them picture the wedding they were considering and become more interested in seeing the venue firsthand.

**The time before a venue tour deserves a place in the advertising strategy.**

A confirmation gives couples the practical details of their appointment. The period before it can also be an opportunity to build anticipation around what they will experience when they arrive.

That is what made the owner's suggestion relevant to our conversation. She brought an idea for showing the venue, and we considered how it could support interest while couples were waiting to come in.

For a venue that already attracts inquiries and schedules visits, this is a useful part of the strategy to make room for. We want to understand the time between those milestones, including what could help a couple look forward to taking the next step in person.

That's the kind of thinking we bring to ELEVATE, our full-service advertising management program. We want an advertising partnership to consider the interest a venue attracts and the opportunity to support it before couples arrive for their tour.
email.ending:

Reply to this email, and let's see what the right next step looks like.

Talk soon,
Whitney

caption.body:
A couple can be interested enough to arrange a tour and still have plenty to discover about the wedding they could have with you. When there's a longer interval before they arrive, some of that discovery could happen during the wait.

That was the opportunity we discussed with a venue owner. She introduced the idea of sharing wedding footage, and our team developed a possible email for the couples who wouldn't be visiting straight away.

The purpose was to give them an earlier sense of the experience they were coming to see. A wedding taking place in the space could offer something different from knowing the appointment's date and time.

I like that the conversation made room for the couple's interest to keep developing. Their inquiry had led to a scheduled visit, but the strategy could still consider what would make that visit feel more appealing before it happened.

That is how we want to think about venue advertising: with attention to the waiting period as well as the moment a couple first reaches out.
caption.hook: There's room to help couples imagine your venue while their visit is still ahead.
caption.ending:
The time before a tour gives us another opportunity to consider what could help a couple look forward to experiencing the venue in person.

-Whitney

When couples can't visit immediately, the time before they arrive can help them become more interested in the wedding they could have with you. We believe that interval deserves consideration in the advertising strategy, alongside the inquiry and the tour itself.

slides.job: Establish the real waiting-period situation without private scheduling details.
slides.text:
This came up in a conversation with a venue owner whose couples sometimes scheduled their visits further out.

We were discussing what could help those couples stay interested before coming in. They had a tour ahead of them, and there was an opportunity to give them something meaningful to anticipate during the wait.

slides.job: Give the owner clear first credit for the video idea.
slides.text:
The owner suggested a wedding video.

Her idea was to give couples a glimpse of a wedding at the venue before they experienced the space for themselves. That offered a possible way to help them imagine the day they were considering while their in-person visit was still some time away.

slides.job: Show our team's contribution in proposal tense.
slides.text:
Our team proposed an additional email for the couples whose tours were further away.

It could share the footage before their visit, making the wait an opportunity to build excitement. The owner brought the video into the discussion; our contribution was a possible place for it in the pre-tour follow-up.

slides.job: Connect the story to the reader's situation without assuming their existing follow-up is inadequate.
slides.text:
For your venue, the tour may be the moment when couples can fully experience what they've been considering.

Before then, they're anticipating a place they haven't yet walked through. That leaves room to help them understand what they're looking forward to, especially when the appointment is further ahead.

slides.job: Explain the purpose of the proposed content, without turning the asset into video instruction.
slides.text:
The proposed footage had a purpose beyond filling an email.

It could help a couple see a wedding taking place in the setting they were coming to visit. That is a way to build on their interest before arrival, giving them more to imagine about the venue and their own day.

slides.job: Deepen the central reframe about the waiting period.
slides.text:
A visit on the calendar gives the couple a next step. The period leading up to it still deserves thought.

We want to consider both: the opportunity to bring someone into the venue and the opportunity to help them remain interested while they wait. Those belong in the same strategic conversation.

slides.job: State WIA's belief with one bold key line.
slides.text:
**We believe the wait before a tour belongs in the advertising strategy.**

Understanding that interval helps us consider what could support the interest a venue attracts. It gives our conversations with owners room to include how couples anticipate a visit, rather than focusing only on how they scheduled it.

slides.job: Close for both support preferences without an offer CTA or self-audit.
slides.text:
Whether you want our team to manage your advertising or launch your campaigns and guide you while you run them, this is the kind of thinking we want beside that work.

The partnership should make room for what happens before couples arrive, including the opportunity to help them become more interested during the wait.

caption.body:
The tour offers a chance to experience your venue firsthand. When couples arrange that visit further ahead, there's also a stretch of time when they can continue imagining what their wedding there might look like.

We explored that interval with a venue owner who suggested using a wedding video. Our team proposed sharing it through a supplemental message before the appointment.

The idea began with her, and the recommendation took shape around the wait. Could that footage give those couples an earlier sense of the venue experience, so they had more to look forward to when they came in?

That is the reason this moment matters to us. A future tour is a meaningful next step, and the advertising discussion can also make space for building interest before it takes place.

We want to understand what couples are moving toward after an inquiry. For a venue, that includes the visit itself and the opportunity to support their anticipation in the days leading up to it.

prior_content_context.argument: We keep upcoming dates in the ad strategy by finding a reason they're right for couples now, including a venue's ability to host a wedding without a long engagement.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners already advertising who are planning their next season's calendar and want their ads to reflect what their team can actually offer couples.
prior_content_context.mechanism: Whitney asked what made spring weddings at the venue appealing, then explored seasonal food and drink. She also proposed explaining that couples didn't need a long engagement because the venue had a team that could pull the wedding together.

prior_content_context.argument: When couples book a venue tour well in advance, the business may need to keep the venue in consideration without expanding into tour times that do not fit its staffing or preparation constraints. A personalized preview before the visit is a possible alternative to treating schedule expansion as the only response.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding-venue owners whose couples book tours more than two weeks ahead and who cannot readily add weekend or early-morning appointments.
prior_content_context.mechanism: The venue owner said couples sometimes found another venue before their scheduled visit, while also describing limits on Saturday tours and drawbacks to Sunday appointments. Whitney proposed a phone or video touchpoint and a supplemental message for people whose tours were booked farther out; these were ideas, not tested interventions.

prior_content_context.argument: We keep the wedding a venue hosts today separate from the one its owner is planning, so the details in its ads match what couples can experience.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners refining their spaces or adding wedding packages who want their ads to represent the business accurately as it grows.
prior_content_context.mechanism: When Carli asked whether to describe her hoped-for wedding or what actually happens, Whitney asked for the current couple's experience. Later, Whitney checked whether proposed patio draping was a future improvement.

prior_content_context.argument: We start by understanding how couples already buy from your wedding business, so our advertising recommendations build on the work you've already done.

prior_content_context.mechanism: Whitney traced the prospect's first inquiry through to an automated information page, checking how calls, texts and emails were answered. prior_content_context.argument: We treat an owner's firsthand knowledge of her weddings as evidence for the ad strategy, even when the search numbers are small.
